canberra.title: AIS marks project milestone for game-changing revitalisation
canberra.snippet: At one point the nation’s premier athlete development program was about to be shipped off to Queensland. Now its ageing campus is o...
canberra.content:
ASC CEO Kieren Perkins with federal Sports Minister Anika Wells, ACT Senator Katy Gallagher and Member for Canberra Alicia Payne, as well as young athletes. Behind them the old athletes village is coming down. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

At one point the nation’s premier athlete development program was about to be shipped off to Queensland. Now its ageing campus is on the way to a $250 million makeover that confirms the Australian Institute of Sport’s place in the national capital and will set it up for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics.

The AIS has announced a significant milestone in its redevelopment program, appointing a construction company and reaching the halfway point in its demolition of buildings no longer considered fit for purpose, including the old athletes village.

Initial construction for the new facilities is planned to begin later this year, with Richard Crookes Construction appointed to deliver the main works. They are expected to be completed in the first half of 2028, providing a four-year runway to the Olympics.

The project will create more than 300 jobs for Canberrans over the course of the build.

The AIS Podium Project is billed as a once-in-a-generation redevelopment of the 75-hectare Bruce campus and the most significant upgrade to the site since it was established in the 1980s.

It will deliver three new state-of-the-art, fully accessible facilities at the northern end of the campus, including new 200-bed multi-storey athletes’ accommodation, an inflatable indoor Multi Sports Dome and High-Performance Testing and Training Centre (HPTTC).

At an event to mark the milestone, Australian Sports Commission CEO Kieren Perkins thanked the Albanese Government for keeping the AIS in Canberra and funding the redevelopment.

“$249.7 million is not a small thing, and we are incredibly grateful that the investment has enabled us to move the AIS forward to ensure that as we look to Brisbane 32 and beyond, Australian athletes will be ready to continue to succeed, and win well for all of us on the international stage,” Mr Perkins said.

The AIS revitalisation is now under way.

The High Performance Testing Centre. Image: ASC.

The fully accessible athlete accommodation. Image: ASC.

The Multi Sports Dome. Image: ASC.

He said the new facilities would boost the AIS’s capacity to take more students and athletes from across the country, and include more sports in its programs.

Mr Perkins said, for example, hard courts for sports such as netball that want to be at the AIS were hard to find at present.

He said the new fully accessible accommodation block would be a game-changer for abled and para-athletes coming to Canberra to train with the best staff and in the best environment.

The facilities that all athletes would be able to use would make an extraordinary difference, including all-year, all-weather training and testing access.

Mr Perkins said this would reinforce the already amazing things the AIS team did in Bruce.

“It will absolutely make a difference, and not just for this generation but for many to come,” he said.

Mr Perkins said the AIS had also opened in the past year its altitude accommodation facility and environmental training facility, which was the largest in the Southern Hemisphere.

The AIS redevelopment is a key part of overall plans for the Bruce precinct, detailed in a Master Plan released on Thursday.

Mr Perkins said the Master Plan opened up a lot of very interesting ideas about how the entire Bruce Precinct can be looked at and the AIS would be working with both the federal and ACT governments as the plan develops.

He said plans for the development of the southern side of the AIS campus would depend on the still to be decided location of the stadium.

It was important that the AIS interacted with the rest of the institutions in the Bruce precinct, especially to be able to share resources.

“I think one of the things that we could all absolutely agree on is that when you have centres of excellence like this, there’s a lot of enthusiasm to be able to build facilities and to have the opportunity to deliver services, research, engineering, and innovation,” Mr Perkins said.

“One thing that we all suffer from is a scarcity of resources, so the more we work together, the more that we’re able to actually ensure that we’re building efficiency, we’re leveraging each other’s capabilities and utilising that best opportunity. It provides a better outcome for all.”

canberra.title: Police catch Kylee McHugh’s alleged killer with DNA, undercover sting
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing details. An accused killer is alleged to have left behind his DNA on his victim’...
canberra.content:
Jack Henry Curtin (right) has been accused of murdering Kylee McHugh (left). Photos: ACT Policing.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing details.

An accused killer is alleged to have left behind his DNA on his victim’s body before undercover police officers caught him admitting to being involved in her murder.

Jack Henry Curtin, 27, was arrested for the alleged murder of 46-year-old Kylee McHugh earlier this week, before Region obtained court documents that outlined the police investigation and the allegations against him.

The documents say a neighbour in the apartment complex on Osborne Place, Belconnen, woke to the smell of fire at around 6:30 am on 18 May 2026 and called Triple Zero.

Firefighters quickly arrived and forced their way into Ms McHugh’s unit before discovering her in her bedroom. She was carried outside, where she was declared deceased.

They also found fire in five locations in her unit: the bathroom, lounge room and laundry, behind the front door and on her bed.

It appeared “ignitable liquid pour patterns” were present at some of these locations.

The documents say a postmortem examination found Ms McHugh had no carbon monoxide or cyanide in her blood, which indicated she died before the fire took hold in the unit.

She also had numerous blunt force injuries to her body, especially her face and neck, as well as possible defensive injuries to her hands. The neck injury was described as severe.

Forensic pathologist Professor Johan Duflou thought her cause of death was the blunt force injuries to her head and neck. He thought there were no indications she was alive when the fire took hold.

When police began making inquiries, they were told a couple had been staying at Ms McHugh’s unit earlier in May 2026, but their relationship deteriorated because the pair accused her of stealing their cannabis.

One person told police this couple was Mr Curtin and his then-partner, 28-year-old Mary Ayuel. The latter was apparently friends with Ms McHugh.

Ms McHugh called ACT Housing, who owned her property, on 13 May to talk about the couple, but Housing told her she’d have to call police to evict the pair.

She said she would, but “once I do that, my life becomes a threat”. She kicked the couple out a couple of days later.

Police escort 27-year-old Jack Henry Curtin into the City Police Station. Photo: ACT Policing.

Police also found numerous messages between Ms McHugh and a phone number, reportedly used by Mr Curtin, between 7 and 15 May.

Two messages to her read, “Go buy some weed to replace mine or prepare yourself when you come back don’t come back not expecting nothing to happen”, and, “Where’s my f-in weed b-h”.

“I have not stolen anything from you,” she later replied.

Police spoke to Mr Curtin a few days after the fire. He allegedly described himself as a “trained fighter, MMA and Krav Maga, Muay Thai” and said he had recently lost his phone.

“I know more events about Kylee … That chick just died and burnt up to a crisp,” he allegedly told police.

Police found CCTV showing Ms McHugh on Howie Court, a street near her home, at around 10 pm on 17 May.

CCTV also allegedly filmed Mr Curtin in Belconnen at around the same time. He was allegedly seen between Howie Court and Osborne Place at around 3:30 am on 18 May, before police spotted him again on Howie Place an hour later.

Police also obtained his DNA. According to the initial results from the forensic examination, police allege his DNA could not be excluded from the samples taken from Ms McHugh’s body, including her genitals.

Then in July 2026, police began an undercover operation into Mr Curtin. During this sting, he is alleged to have made admissions about the murder.

He was arrested on 7 September. When he was formally interviewed, police said he gave “contrasting versions of the evidence provided to him”, although he did not make any admissions to the alleged murder or arson.

He did reportedly admit being in the area at the time of the alleged offences, as he said he saw a “glow” at Ms McHugh’s unit, before returning later to see a fire at her home.

Mr Curtin was charged with murder and arson before he was refused bail when he faced the ACT Magistrates Court this week.

The matter was adjourned to 6 October. No pleas were entered.

canberra.title: Police and Customs to get new powers in fight against illegal tobacco
canberra.snippet: New laws to crack down on the illegal tobacco trade will beef up government powers in the intensifying fight against the black market. La...
canberra.content:
Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill says current tobacco customs laws were designed for another era. Photo: Region.

New laws to crack down on the illegal tobacco trade will beef up government powers in the intensifying fight against the black market.

Labor is amending both the Customs Act and the Proceeds of Crime Act, with legislation to grant law enforcement agencies stronger powers to detect, investigate and disrupt illicit tobacco activity and choke off the profits to organised crime.

Border Force and police forces around the country will be able to move against suppliers of illegal tobacco products more easily on suspicion, dictated by “observable indicators” outlined in the legislation.

Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill said government agencies will have the tools they need to make the illicit trade less profitable and higher risk for organised crime.

“Anyone involved in the illegal tobacco trade – whether high up in the crime groups, mid-level operatives, distributors or those running and working in the shops – would be wise to get a new job and do so quickly,” he said.

“These new laws will be a powerful tool for the Australian Border Force and all state and territory police to go after serious and organised crime, and may be used against retail operators, as well as other companies involved in the trade.

“Prosecutions were often frustrated under the old offences, as authorities were frequently required to prove that tobacco was imported with ‘intent’ to defraud the revenue.

“It will soon be easier for law enforcement to punish those involved in the illicit tobacco trade as this Bill introduces a list of ‘observable indicators’ such as non-compliant packaging or products, concealing tobacco to avoid detection or if the sales price is below the excise and GST combined.

“If any one of these indicators is established, it is taken to satisfy the reasonable suspicion test for the relevant offence.”

Amendments to the Customs Act will close regulatory loopholes exploited by criminals by introducing new offences relating to the unlawful importation, possession and movement of tobacco products.

That will reduce the need to prove an intention to evade tobacco duties

The changes will also restore customs control over duty-refundable tobacco held in licensed warehouses until it is lawfully sold, exported or otherwise removed from the duty-refund system

The notification, seizure, forfeiture and destruction of illicit tobacco products will be streamlined; and new licensing and compliance conditions will be introduced for customs brokers, depots and warehouses authorised to handle tobacco products.

Amendments to the Proceeds of Crime Act will make it easier for authorities to obtain documents and other information relevant to criminal investigations and court proceedings.

They will boost provisions for calculating and recovering financial benefits derived from criminal conduct, including through confiscation orders and strengthen unexplained wealth laws by improving how authorities identify and recover assets that cannot be linked to legitimate income.

Mr Hill said Australia’s current tobacco customs laws were designed for another era with low-level criminals and minor revenue evasion.

Today, he said, the scale and complexity of organised crime groups demands a new approach to going after anyone involved in the illicit tobacco market.

“It’s modernising our customs laws to confront the nature and the scale of the problem that the world and Australia face with illegal tobacco,” the Assistant Minister said.

“This is weaponised now by these transnational serious organised crime syndicates. They’re big multinational endeavours, and they just want to make money.

“It’s a global problem. Australia’s not immune. They’ve got this cheap stuff they make for less than $1 a pack and flood national borders, and they’ve set up these supply chains and retail networks.”

He said the reforms help curb the illegal trade while also protecting honest businesses that “do the right thing”, as well as the community.

Government agencies have recently conducted coordinated raids across the country on targeted retail outlets, seizing large quantities of illegal tobacco products.

Labor insists that law enforcement is the way to tackle the illicit tobacco issue.

The Coalition last week released a policy proposal to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent to stamp out the illegal trade.

If implemented, the Coalition’s plan would reduce the excise on a standard packet of 20 cigarettes from about $30 to just $6, dramatically removing the price advantage currently enjoyed by the black market.

One Nation has presented a similar proposal.

But the government is having no part of it, saying it will not be in a “race to the bottom” with organised crime.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said while he hadn’t yet seen the new legislation, he was standing by his reduce-the-excise policy.

“If you want to destroy the business model of illicit tobacco in this country, the organised crime, the gangs that are behind it, you have to take the profit and the customers away from it,” he said.

canberra.title: Deputy steps up as the new CPSU national secretary
canberra.snippet: The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) has a new national secretary, replacing Melissa Donnelly who was recently elected to head up...
canberra.content:
Rebecca Fawcett has been appointed CPSU national secretary. Photo: CPSU.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) has a new national secretary, replacing Melissa Donnelly who was recently elected to head up the ACTU.

Rebecca Fawcett has been promoted from CPSU deputy secretary to the top job, taking up the appointment of national secretary on Thursday (10 September).

A meeting of the union’s governing council made the appointment, noting that Ms Fawcett is the CPSU’s first working single mother to serve as national secretary. She is also the fourth woman to hold the role.

The CPSU’s governing council is directly elected by CPSU members and sets the union’s strategic direction and objectives.

It is currently meeting in Adelaide to discuss artificial intelligence and automated decision-making in government agencies; bringing public sector work back in-house; and progress in APS-wide bargaining.

Ms Fawcett joined the CPSU as an organiser in 2001, and has played a central role in major union campaigns, including the Your Rights at Work campaign against the Howard government’s WorkChoices laws.

“I am incredibly proud to be appointed national secretary of the CPSU and to continue standing alongside members right across the public sector,” she said on her appointment.

“CPSU members do essential work for the Australian community every single day. They deserve secure jobs, fair pay, safe workplaces, and public services that are properly staffed, properly funded and properly valued.

“Together, we have won important improvements, but there is more to do.

“We will keep fighting to bring public sector work back in-house, strengthen protections around AI and automated decision-making, and make sure workers have the pay and conditions they need during a cost-of-living crisis.

“Our union is strongest when members and delegates are at the centre of every decision we make.

“I will always be focused on making sure members’ workplace issues and concerns are heard and acted on.”

In her more than two decades in the CPSU, Ms Fawcett has held senior roles across the union, including as national organiser for the Defence Department, legal director and deputy secretary.

She has negotiated numerous enterprise agreements and oversaw the CPSU’s national legal and industrial work, including its landmark Same Job Same Pay case in the Australian Taxation Office.

Ms Fawcett has led campaigns to protect regional jobs by stopping the closure of Australian Electoral Commission offices in regional Australia and helped stop attempts to privatise Airservices Australia firefighting functions.

She has also coordinated APS-wide industrial action to defend workplace rights and convened the CPSU’s AI reference group, which is leading the union’s approach to artificial intelligence.

As the CPSU’s lead in the first round of APS-wide bargaining, Ms Fawcett and her team secured several wins for public sector workers, including flexible work and working-from-home rights; genuinely negotiated pay increases; and 18 weeks paid parental leave for both parents.

Other improvements included stronger consultation rights, significant pay increases for the lowest-paid APS workers, 25 per cent casual loading, and new leave entitlements.

Last week, while still in the deputy’s role, Ms Fawcett called on the Federal Government to impose an immediate pause on complex automated decisions until APS-wide rules are put in place.

She said the government needed to develop “clear and mandatory safeguards” for the public service.

“Public sector workers understand better than anyone the risks of rolling out complex automated decision-making systems without proper safeguards, transparency and accountability,” Ms Fawcett said.

“The lesson from Robodebt is clear – government must not allow complex automated decision-making to operate ahead of clear rules that protect people, uphold public service values and ensure decisions can be properly explained and challenged.

“When frontline workers are consulted and genuinely listened to, governments make better decisions. Workers can identify practical risks and unintended consequences before they become serious problems for the community.”

canberra.title: New Zealand tip-off resulted in child abuse charges against ACT man
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. Distributing allegations first reported to New Zealand Police ultimately res...
canberra.content:
10 September 2026

The allegations against the 39-year-old Canberra man were first reported to New Zealand Police. Photo: New Zealand Police Facebook.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

Distributing allegations first reported to New Zealand Police ultimately resulted in a man being charged with allegedly abusing a child in the ACT.

The 39-year-old man from Canberra has now been refused bail twice, although he has said he will fight the allegations.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the man was alleged to have repeatedly sexually assaulted a girl, who is related to him, multiple times between 2018 and 2020.

The alleged incidents were initially reported to police in New Zealand before ACT Policing arrested the man in August.

He was originally refused bail before he applied to be released again in the ACT Magistrates Court on Tuesday (8 September), which prosecutor Ahmad Mufti opposed.

Mr Mufti said the alleged offending was clearly predatory and against a vulnerable person.

“The offending shows an entrenched pattern of offending in relation to a child,” he alleged.

He alleged in some cases, the man had isolated the child in order to assault her.

Mr Mufti also said his office was reviewing whether it was appropriate to lay a charge of the persistent sexual abuse of a child, which carries a maximum sentence of 25 years’ jail.

He ultimately said he opposed bail on the alleged risk the man posed to children in general.

“He can’t be trusted to be on conditional liberty around any children,” the prosecutor alleged.

The man’s lawyer, Zachary McBride of Owen McBride, said the allegations were historical in nature and proposed his client be granted bail on conditions, including that he not be alone with someone under 18.

He said his client could live with his employer, who was aware of the allegations and would continue his employment.

Mr McBride also argued that as his client had no prior criminal history, he should be given the benefit of the doubt and granted bail.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt said the man was presumed innocent, but the allegations outlined ongoing offending as well as a “flagrant disregard for the well-being of the child”.

She was concerned about “some degree of pattern” in the allegations and the alleged general risk to the community if he was released.

Bail was refused and the matter was adjourned to October.

The man has entered pleas of not guilty to two counts each of committing an act of indecency on a person under 16 and incest on a person under 16, as well as to single counts of committing an act of indecency on a person under 10, grooming and assault.

He has not been named to protect the girl’s identity.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

australia.title: Grace Tame apologises for comments labelling rape of Israeli women during Hamas attacks ‘propaganda’
australia.snippet: The former Australian of the Year said she stood with survivors of sexual violence ‘everywhere’ and ‘no matter who they are’ Get our brea...
australia.content:
Grace Tame has apologised for her comments labelling the rape of Israeli women by Hamas during the 7 October attacks as “propaganda” and “debunked”, saying her words were “misinterpreted”.

The former Australian of the Year issued the apology in an Instagram video on Thursday. The comments were made in an ABC interview about Israel and Gaza in March.

In the video, Tame said she stood with survivors of sexual violence “everywhere, no matter who they are”.

“There’s something I’ve wanted to clarify for a while, which I regret not clarifying sooner. I stand with survivors of sexual violence everywhere, no matter who they are”, she said.

“Comments I made on ABC radio in March this year were misinterpreted to mean that I disbelieve Israeli survivors of sexual violence. This is not the case. I always have, and always will stand with survivors of sexual violence,” she said.

Tame said Human Rights Watch had been unable to find evidence to support the claim that Israeli women were raped en masse on 7 October 2023.

“However, I do not deny the legitimate accusations of rape made by individual Israeli women, including accounts of gang-rape,” she said.

“I do not hate Israelis. I do not hate Jewish people. I abhor the crimes of the State of Israel.

“I believe Israeli survivors, I believe Jewish survivors, as I believe all survivors. While the intention of my remarks was not to imply otherwise, I acknowledge and sincerely apologise for any harm their mischaracterisation has caused.”

Lynda Ben-Menashe, the president of the National Council of Jewish Women Australia, lashed Tame’s statement, saying it was not an apology.

“She called Israeli women’s widely proven claims of sexual violence ‘debunked propaganda,’ which added insult to their injury, and fanned the flames of incitement against all Jewish women – and men in this country,” she said in a statement.

“Saying she’s sorry for how people interpreted her words is not an apology. It neither rehabilitates her nor reverses the damage her original words did to us.”

In the March interview, Tame was asked whether she had expressed outrage about Israeli women who were sexually assaulted during the 7 October attacks.

She said: “I’m not going to sink to the level of entertaining any kind of propaganda” and that “those things have been debunked”.

In 2024, the United Nation’s special envoy on sexual violence in conflict concluded there were “reasonable grounds” to believe sexual assaults including rape and gang-rape in several places took place during the 7 October attacks by Hamas.

Tame’s comments drew a rebuke from the Israeli embassy in Canberra, with a social media post accusing her of losing her “moral compass”.

The ABC’s ombudsman’s office said it received 145 complaints after Tame’s interview, while a further four raised “distinct but similar matters”.

australia.title: RSL says One Nation’s Hastie ‘slur’ was an ‘attack on every veteran’s service’ – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Labor introducing new laws to crack down on illegal tobacco Labor will introduce new laws to make it easier to pr...
australia.content:
RSL Australia says calling a veteran a traitor is a ‘slur’

Sarah Basford Canales

Australia’s largest veteran support group has warned calling veterans traitors is a “slur” and an attack on every veteran’s service.

It follows a bitter rift between the Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie and the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, after the latter refused to apologise for a cartoon her party published that labelled Hastie a “traitor”.

In a statement this afternoon, the Returned & Services League of Australia, better known as RSL Australia, said using the word sends a “corrosive message to the wider veteran community” that “your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient”.

The statement said:

The recent comments from Senator Hanson towards Andrew Hastie MP go beyond political disagreement.

This may have begun as a political dispute between Senator Hanson and Mr Hastie, however, when a person’s military service is used as the punchline, when the word ‘traitor’ is thrown at someone who has worn the uniform and deployed on operations, that stops being politics and starts being an attack on every veteran’s service.

Veterans don’t stop being accountable to their oath once they leave the ADF. Branding a former soldier a ‘traitor’ sends a corrosive message to the wider veteran community: that your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient.

RSL Australia asks all sides of politics to keep that distinction. Calling a veteran a traitor is a slur, and it deserves to be treated as one regardless of who it’s aimed at or how it’s dressed up.”

What we learned, Thursday 10 September

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today!

Before we say bye, let’s recap the day’s top headlines.

  • Former prime minister Kevin Rudd did the rounds in Canberra today for a round of high-profile speeches this week, marking his return to Australia after serving as ambassador to Washington DC.

  • The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has warned the Albanese government not to join the “madness” of cutting migration to appease One Nation. Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has backed the warnings.

  • Andrew Hastie has continued to step up the fight against One Nation, after one of its cartoon Please Explain videos referred to the Liberal MP and SAS veteran as a “traitor” after he gave evidence against Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation claim.

  • Jacqui Lambie, an independent senator and defence veteran, has also joined the criticism against Pauline Hanson .

  • Moira Deeming, the former Victorian Liberal MP, has announced she will lead the conservative Family First party at the November state election.

  • Angus Taylor has confirmed the Coalition won’t support the government’s digital duty of care bill in its current form, because it would enforce political censorship.

  • A controversial plan for the Minns government to allow big industry to use a new Great Koala national park to offset its climate pollution will go ahead after a deal with the Greens.

  • Australian-first laws that guarantee the right to work from home two days a week are unlikely to pass Victorian parliament before the November state election, with the Coalition and crossbench teaming up to refer the bill to an inquiry.

  • The high court has refused with costs an appeal by women-only app Giggle against a full federal court ruling in May that upheld a landmark decision that the app and its founder, Sall Grover unlawfully discriminated against Roxanne Tickle after the transgender woman was denied access to the platform.

  • And finally, here’s a Tl;dr on what happened in question time.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning!

Benita Kolovos

Victorian premier says Liberals have shown ‘true colours’ on work from home

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, says the Liberals have “shown their true colours” by voting with crossbenchers to refer work from home laws to a parliamentary inquiry.

After pretending to support our work from home laws all the way along, the Liberal party have teamed up with the One Nation party and voted our work from home laws down …

This legislation has been in the Parliament for three months. I met with the business community and made it fair for families and fair for employers. The Liberal party and Jess Wilson have shown their true colours.

The inquiry will report back on 20 October, a few weeks before the government enters caretaker mode.

Carroll indicated he would not recall parliament, saying he already added an extra week:

I’ve already added a week to get all of our integrity legislation through. It was always designed to be going through this week, I delayed to get the business community the consultation they wanted.

The Liberal Party had been very clear: we will pass this. And what have they done? Behind Victorians’ backs, behind the government’s back, done a sneaky deal with One Nation. If you needed any more proof that the Liberal Party are anti-worker, look what they did right now to working women, to working families that work hard every day and just want the right to work from home.

VIC Property Council welcomes delays to the WFH Bill

The Property Council has welcomed delays the Victoria’s national-leading work from home bill after the Coalition and crossbenchers decided to refer it to an inquiry, effectively stalling it until after the election.

The organisation said the draft legislation requires “further scrutiny given the complexity and legal challenges it presents to all Victorians.”

In a statement, Victorian Executive Director Cath Evans said the decision was the only correct choice.

The Victorian Parliament has seen sense. Instead of forcing rushed legislation through Parliament, it has made the right call by sending the Bill to a Committee to properly examine its operation, implications and legal validity.

Referring the Bill to a Committee gives the Parliament the opportunity to methodically examine all of the legal and economic issues associated with the Bill.

This decision should be the clearest signal: the Victorian Government needs to be focused on the things that will actually drive growth - building more homes, creating jobs, attracting investment and restoring confidence in the state.

We hope this is the beginning of a more constructive approach to addressing the economic issues facing Victoria, and a government that listens to business and recognises that employers and employees are best placed to agree on arrangements that work for them.”

Boats seized, mud crabs freed in seafood sting

Boats have been seized and mud crabs freed in a crackdown on black market seafood trafficking, AAP reports.

Three boats will be destroyed after successful prosecutions involving illegal seafood trafficking in Moreton Bay, the Gold Coast and Brisbane. Two offenders were caught by Queensland Boating and Fisheries Patrol officers selling seafood outside the state’s commercial fishing system.

A Russell Island man was fined $10,000 for black market sales of mud crabs, king threadfin salmon and mulloway. Officers also located 139 protected bivalve molluscs and an undersized mud crab in his possession.

The man was ordered to forfeit the vessel and associated equipment.

It follows two other successful prosecutions of illegal seafood harvesting in southeast Queensland, with all three forfeited vessels to be crushed. Officers executed a search warrant and seized his vessel, trailer, outboard motor and marine electronics.

Deputy Director-General Fisheries and Forestry Pauline Jacob said the offenders weren’t simply catching a few extra fish for dinner. She said:

They were profiting from Queensland’s fisheries resources through ongoing illegal seafood sales that undermine honest commercial fishers and legitimate seafood businesses.

She said licensed commercial fishers invest heavily to meet strict licensing, sustainability and food safety requirements.

Black market operators avoid those costs while undercutting businesses that do the right thing.

Queenslanders deserve confidence that the seafood they buy has been legally harvested, responsibly managed and supplied through legitimate businesses.

RSL Australia says calling a veteran a traitor is a ‘slur’

Sarah Basford Canales

Australia’s largest veteran support group has warned calling veterans traitors is a “slur” and an attack on every veteran’s service.

It follows a bitter rift between the Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie and the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, after the latter refused to apologise for a cartoon her party published that labelled Hastie a “traitor”.

In a statement this afternoon, the Returned & Services League of Australia, better known as RSL Australia, said using the word sends a “corrosive message to the wider veteran community” that “your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient”.

The statement said:

The recent comments from Senator Hanson towards Andrew Hastie MP go beyond political disagreement.

This may have begun as a political dispute between Senator Hanson and Mr Hastie, however, when a person’s military service is used as the punchline, when the word ‘traitor’ is thrown at someone who has worn the uniform and deployed on operations, that stops being politics and starts being an attack on every veteran’s service.

Veterans don’t stop being accountable to their oath once they leave the ADF. Branding a former soldier a ‘traitor’ sends a corrosive message to the wider veteran community: that your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient.

RSL Australia asks all sides of politics to keep that distinction. Calling a veteran a traitor is a slur, and it deserves to be treated as one regardless of who it’s aimed at or how it’s dressed up.”

Read more:

High court refuses Giggle’s appeal over women-only app discrimination

Josh Taylor

The high court has refused with costs an appeal by women-only app Giggle against a full federal court ruling in May that upheld a landmark decision that the app and its founder, Sall Grover unlawfully discriminated against Roxanne Tickle after the transgender woman was denied access to the platform.

The full court had upheld the lower court’s decision that Giggle and Grover had indirectly discriminated against Tickle when she was barred from the platform because they thought she was a man.

The full court doubled the initial amount of damages awarded to Tickle to $20,000.

Grover’s team had argued the app – designed as a “women-only safe space” – constituted a “special measure” under the Sex Discrimination Act (SDA), which allows discrimination with the aim of redressing historical disadvantage between men and women.

The high court said there was “no reason to doubt” the full court’s construction of the relevant sections of the Sex Discrimination Act, and any appeal on these provisions “has insufficient prospects of success” to warrant granting a special leave to appeal the case to the high court.

It brings to an end the long-running legal saga, which commenced in 2022.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said in May in a video posted to social media featuring Grover, that the Coalition was committed to “amending the Sex Discrimination Act to ensure protections for single-sex spaces are based on biological sex,” if elected.

Victoria’s WFH bill effectively delayed until after state election

Benita Kolovos

Australian-first laws that guarantee the right to work from home two days a week are unlikely to pass Victorian parliament before the November state election, with the Coalition and crossbench teaming up to refer the bill to an inquiry.

The laws were first announced in 2025 by the then premier Jacinta Allan in a bid to capitalise on the backlash to the federal Coalition’s plan to force public servants back into the office full-time, which contributed to their election loss.

The Victorian Coalition, though, had said it would support the bill and expected it would pass parliament on Thursday.

But in a shock development, the Coalition has joined with crossbench MPs, including Legalise Cannabis, David Limbrick from the Libertarians, former Liberal MP Moira Deeming and One Nation’s Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell to refer the bill to an inquiry that effectively stalls it until after the election.

The inquiry was put forward by Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Jeff Bourman and passed 18 votes to 17.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all so much for joining me on the politics blog this week!

I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok and see you here bright and early Monday.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The PM’s honorary membership at a golf club that received $6m in funding from an invite-only grants program was a focus of question time today, including why a Daily Telegraph article from 2019 highlighted the honorary membership but the PM claimed he didn’t know he even had it.

  • Anthony Albanese ended up ignoring several of the questions and gave somewhat unrelated answers.

  • Independents Sophie Scamps and Helen Haines asked the government why Australia won’t join partners including the UK in implementing a trade ban on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – Albanese and Richard Marles repeated the same lines that Penny Wong gave yesterday.

  • Two MPs – Nationals MP Kevin Hogan and Labor backbencher Basem Abdo – were kicked out in the middle of a question to Jim Chalmers about government debt bonds.

Josh Taylor

Department denies dereliction of duties over alleged AI hallucinations in submission on social media ban

Last month, the federal infrastructure department was quizzed in a Senate inquiry over claims made in a submission to the social media ban amendment bill that alleged citation errors identified in the age assurance technology trial report were AI hallucinations.

It was aired just before we published our story identifying several errors in the report.

At the time, officials relayed the claims by ACCS - the age verification organisation that undertook the trial - that the errors were due to links breaking in the intervening time between the report publication and the hearing.

Senator Fatima Payman queried in her dissenting report of the inquiry whether officials had been derelict in their duty in not independently verifying the advice provided by ACCS at the time.

The department’s secretary, Jim Betts, said in a letter to the committee chair, tabled this week, that officials are not failing in their duties if they give evidence “based on advice provided to them that, at face value, can be accepted as accurate”.

Betts said:

The representations made by officials were based on information available to them at the time and were honestly and reasonably held.

Betts said the department had continued to investigate since then. The department said ACCS had since provided new citations to replace the erroneous ones and would correct the report online.

ACCS has denied the citation errors were AI hallucinations.

The department declined to answer further questions on the report.

That’s time on question time

After a final question to the prime minister, Anthony Albanese calls time on QT for the week.

Coalition tries to pin Albanese on golf club membership

Take two – Anthony Albanese is asked again how the Daily Telegraph knew about his honorary membership in 2019 but he didn’t, and asks if it’s just “another case of you falling off a stage?”

The inference there is that Albanese is lying about the membership and doesn’t want to own up to it (like when he tried to deny that he fell off a stage during the last election campaign).

Albanese once again does his absolute best to totally avoid the question.

He says the article was related to a 2019 campaign to save the golf course from future development, and does a little copy and paste from a previous answer where he said that of the Coalition’s 2025 election promises, not one was for Sydney’s inner west.

I certainly supported it as did people throughout the area of the inner west either side of the Cooks River, because this is an absolutely vital and precious piece of the inner west, of Sydney.

The manager of opposition business, Dan Tehan, tries to table the article to parliament, but leader of the House, Tony Burke rejects the attempt, and says it’s already online.

Richard Marles offers no further insight on position over Israeli settlements

The independent MP Helen Haines asks: what will it take for Australia to join our allies in imposing trade bans on Israeli settlements in the West Bank?

This time the deputy PM Richard Marles takes the question and sheds no further light on the issue than when Anthony Albanese was asked about it a short time ago.

Multiple nations, including the UK, have announced they’ll implement bans on trade from illegal settlements.

Marles says the Australian government supports a two-state solution, and illegal settlements are hindering that, but that targeted sanctions on individuals and entities are still the answer.

Because of the positions that we have taken, we have put in place sanctions and bans in respect of those that have been participating in the settler – settlements – in the territories, and that has included Israeli ministers themselves. We will continue to look at further targeted measures, working collaboratively with our allies and partners around the world in respect of this issue.

Albanese dodges question on 2019 report of honorary membership in golf club

The opposition has come with receipts, asking how a Daily Telegraph article from 2019 reported that Anthony Albanese was an honorary member of the Marrickville golf club but the prime minister himself didn’t know until now.

A Coalition MP shouts asking if Toto is a member too, to which Albanese replies, smiling: “Don’t attack Toto, you’ve got to draw the line somewhere.”

The prime minister doesn’t really answer the question.

He goes off on a bit of a tangent, saying that the golf club wasn’t even in his electorate in 2019, and that he has the second-smallest electorate in the country.

There is very little green space in my electorate, and I defends every inch of it. In 2019, the Marrickville golf course was not in my electorate. It was actually in the electorate of Barton.

PM on the defensive over Marrickville golf club grant

The prime minister is again on the back foot, defending a $6m grant given to the Marrickville golf club, which he was an honorary member of.

Yesterday Anthony Albanese said the money was to stop sewerage from the club ending up in the Cooks River. Liberal frontbencher Tony Pasin asks if the PM mislead parliament because $1m was used on stormwater works, but $4.55m was spent on a clubhouse precinct.

Albanese provides a pretty short answer, and doesn’t address the substance of the question, but basically does confirm that part of the funding, not all of it, was for the sewerage works.

There were three commitments in my electorate. One for a women’s health centre, the one for a St Vincent de Paul facility, a refuge, for women and children escaping domestic violence, and one for the upgrade of the inner west council–owned Marrickville golf club. Included in that was funding to fix the sewerage because it goes into the river and causes a problem when it floods.

Albanese defends not declaring golf club membership

Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell is next and asks the prime minister why he hasn’t declared his honorary membership of the Marrickville golf club when he did declare honorary membership of the Royal Sydney golf club.

The former received $6m under an invite-only grants program that gave the majority of funding to safe, marginal or target Labor seats.

Spoiler alert: the opposition intervenes three times because they’re not happy with the answer.

Anthony Albanese says it’s because he knew about one (Royal Sydney) but didn’t know about the other, and doesn’t even have a card for the Marrickville club.

Albanese then tries to turn the attention back to the Coalition, and says he took a look at all the opposition’s 2025 election funding promises (which some staff member would have spent many hours trying to pour through).

I looked through the list of Coalition election commitments from 2025 and there were over 1,000 projects worth $1.2bn. I looked for anything in Grayndler and of the thousand projects, there wasn’t a single one in the inner west, not one.

australia.title: Victoria’s historic work from home laws have unexpectedly stalled. Will they survive?

Australian-first laws that guarantee the right to work from home two days a week are unlikely to pass Victorian parliament before the November state election, with the Coalition and crossbench teaming up to refer the bill to an inquiry.

The laws were first announced in 2025 by the then premier Jacinta Allan in a bid to capitalise on the backlash to the federal Coalition’s plan to force public servants back into the office full-time, which contributed to the opposition’s election loss.

The Victorian Coalition, though, had said it would support the bill and expected it would pass parliament on Thursday. But in a shock development, it joined with crossbench MPs to effectively stall the proposed laws until after the election.

Here’s what we know.

australia.title: Jacqui Lambie calls Pauline Hanson an ‘angry little woman’ after One Nation cartoon calling Andrew Hastie a traitor
australia.snippet: Lambie, a veteran and Tasmanian senator, says One Nation leader is a ‘coward’ who is showing her ‘true colours’ Follow our Australia news...
australia.content:
Jacqui Lambie has escalated her attack on Pauline Hanson, describing her as an “angry little woman” and a “bloody coward” after Hanson refused to apologise for or take down a One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie a “traitor”.

Lambie, a crossbencher and army veteran herself, defended Hastie on Thursday, after he called on Hanson to take ownership for a One Nation animated cartoon on social media in which he is repeatedly described as a traitor for giving evidence against Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation case.

Senior Liberals and RSL Australia also joined condemnation of the cartoon on Thursday, with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, calling for it to be taken down.

Hastie has challenged Hanson and Nationals defector Barnaby Joyce to take responsibility for the One Nation video, promising a costly political battle.

Lambie told ABC radio the cartoon should be immediately taken down and that Hanson was now showing her “true colours”.

“What she’s doing in those cartoons is absolutely disgusting. They are full of bloody violence,” Lambie said.

“But attacking Andrew Hastie, a veteran that has served in our Afghanistan war, or any other veteran, is the lowest ebb you can possibly do. That woman is nothing less than a bloody coward.

“I tell you what, you’re seeing her true colours start to shine now. You watch this, the Australian people. Here comes coward Hanson … And any veteran out there thinking about voting for One Nation or standing for them, I tell you what, you had better think twice.”

Later on Thursday, Lambie joined News24 where she launched an extraordinary tirade against the Queensland senator over her track record on veterans.

“She’s dividing this country. She is dividing it. She’s not uniting it. She’s an angry little woman with so much baggage on her that everybody else and her supporters think that is acceptable behaviour, and think it’s everybody else’s fault besides theirs.”

Hastie is an SAS veteran and served twice in Afghanistan but has attracted the ire of One Nation and Hanson’s billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart, after he gave evidence against Roberts-Smith in a failed defamation case against Nine newspapers.

Hanson and Rinehart say Roberts-Smith is being unfairly targeted over war crimes allegations related to his service between 2009 and 2012.

Hastie on Thursday ruled out legal action against Hanson, due to Rinehart’s backing.

“I think it shows [Hanson] to be weak and glass-jawed. I gave her the opportunity to either own her words publicly or to take it down. She chose neither,” he told ABC radio.

“She’s not fit to govern this country. And she’s also cast a massive slur on veterans around the country who think that Australian soldiers should hold high standards of conduct on the battlefield.

“I’m not after legal action, particularly when she’s financed by Australia’s richest person. Why would I walk into a fight that I can’t win financially? But yes, I’m going to impose costs politically.”

Hanson again claimed she had not personally called Hastie a coward, despite posting the video on her social media accounts. Yesterday she told The Nightly newspaper that she would call Hastie a “wanker” instead.

Taylor also called on Hanson to take down the cartoon during a press conference, and said it was wrong for it to remain online.

“Andrew Hastie has served this country with distinction as an officer in the SAS. She should take it down,” Taylor said.

The opposition leader declined to back Hastie’s description of Hanson as “weak and glass-jawed”.

RSL Australia said calling a veteran a “traitor” was a “slur” and sent a “corrosive message” that “your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient”.

“This may have begun as a political dispute between Senator Hanson and Mr Hastie, however, when a person’s military service is used as the punchline, when the word ‘traitor’ is thrown at someone who has worn the uniform and deployed on operations, that stops being politics and starts being an attack on every veteran’s service,” the group said.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge also blasted Hanson, telling News24 it was disgraceful to attack the Liberal frontbencher for giving evidence to a trial under oath.

“I disagree with pretty much everything that comes out of Hastie’s mouth, like his whole suite of policies are things that I tend to oppose … but for the life of me, I can’t work out how any political party can stand by an attack on somebody because they go into court and they tell the truth as they understand it,” he said.

“I mean, it’s actually pretty fucking disgraceful to attack him for that.”

James Paterson, the shadow defence minister, said Hanson and her strategist James Ashby “should be ashamed of themselves”.

“I would never dream of accusing someone who has served in uniform for our country of being a traitor,” he said.

“There’s no graver accusation to make, particularly about someone like Andrew Hastie. Andrew Hastie signed up to the ADF after 9/11. He signed up to fight Islamist terrorists as part of the global war on terror. He served on the frontlines in Afghanistan over multiple tours. What service has anyone in One Nation given that compares in any way, shape or form to Andrew Hastie’s service?”

australia.title: Sydney man jailed for 3.5 years over fake defence reports prepared for Chinese spies
australia.snippet: Alexander Csergo sentenced over reckless foreign interference after preparing documents for duo who approached him on LinkedIn Get our br...
australia.content:
A seemingly innocuous message on a social media platform has snowballed into a Sydney man being jailed for foreign interference.

Alexander Csergo, 58, was jailed for three years and six months on Thursday, after being found guilty by a jury in March of helping Chinese spies.

With time served, he will be eligible for parole in October.

Between May and December 2022, the business owner knew he was assisting Chinese operatives – known only as Ken and Evelyn – when he prepared fake, plagiarised reports about Australia’s defence arrangements, the New South Wales district court judge Craig Smith said on Thursday.

His relationship with the pair began after the Australian IT consultant was approached on LinkedIn by a woman claiming to be from a Chinese thinktank in November 2021.

Csergo, who was living and working in China at the time, should have known Ken and Evelyn were working for China’s ministry of state security, his trial had heard.

But Smith found it was not proven that Csergo was reckless about the prospect of helping the foreign power from the moment he read the message.

“Spotting Chinese intelligence operatives on that program requires training on what to look for,” the judge said.

The 58-year-old Australian used open-source information to compile reports on a variety of topics, including lithium mining, German politics, defence and security. He was specifically asked to dig up private information about Australia’s involvement in the Quad security group and the Aukus deal, Smith said.

He also falsely claimed he had interviewed a number of individuals, including the former prime minister and Mandarin speaker Kevin Rudd, his trial had heard.

The reports were handed to Ken or Evelyn in person – sometimes at restaurants and cafes devoid of other people – in exchange for envelopes containing the equivalent of thousands of dollars in cash.

While the information was worthless, the jury accepted prosecution submissions that the relationship with Csergo and his contacts was valuable.

“I do not consider what he did can be described as overly sophisticated,” Smith said.

“But there was certainly a degree of sophistication around the extensive nature of what he did.”

Ken also handed Csergo a “shopping list” of sensitive topics to research when he returned to Australia in early 2023. However, the judge said there was no evidence Csergo carried out any espionage relating to the list.

Ultimately, Smith ruled it was important to deter the wider community from being wooed into compromising Australia’s national security.

world.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
world.snippet: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ Uganda is withdrawing f...
world.content:
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.

The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

world.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
world.snippet: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mother...
world.content:
Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.

Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.

Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.

Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”

The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.

While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.

“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.

The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

world.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
world.snippet: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali...
world.content:
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”

According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”

Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.

Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.

The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.

“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

world.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
world.snippet: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive hea...
world.content:
Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.

This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

world.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
world.snippet: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known...
world.content:
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.

The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.

The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.

The verdict is subject to appeal.

Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.
